entry.title: Python for AI 102
entry.content:
:round_pushpin: Acknowledgement: This post is based mainly on Dr. Quang-Vinh Dinh’s presentation and slides and partly on peers’ responses from the course, AIO2025, offered by AI VIETNAM.

:thought_balloon: Relevant information and opinions: The audience of this lecture were those who learned Python for AI 101, have some coding experience, and know a bit of AI knowledge. It is reccommended that complete newbies should read the materials and spend time practicing writing code without the assistance of AI over and over again to improve their coding and code-reading skills. Note that only necessary Python knowledge is introduced here.

When you get a result that is not what you expect, do not ask for help immediately. Instead, run the code by hand to figure out where you logic breaks, modify the program, and run it again. Repeat this process and your skills will improve without you noticing it. -Dr. Quang-Vinh Dinh

In today’s post, we’ll look at common errors and loops in Python.

:mag_right: Common Errors

If you tried some Python exercises, you probably have encountered some of the errors we’ll mention shortly.

:one: NameError

NameError occurs when you try to use a variable or function that hasn’t been defined.

a = 7 
Print(a)

c = a + b
print(c)

def a_function(x): 
    a_variable = 4
    return x * a_variable

print(a_variable)

:two: SyntaxError

:three: ZeroDivisorError

a = 7
b = 0
c = a / b
print(c)

:four: TypeError

:five: IndexError

a_list = [1, "love", "aivietnam"]
print(a_list[3])

:six: IndentationError

a = 7 
    b = 8

print(b)

:seven: ValueError

:eight: ModuleNotFoundError

import mymodule

print("iloveaivietnam")

:nine: RecursionError

def a_function(n):
    return a_function(n)

a_function(7)

exercise

Practice Exercises 

# Exercise 1
numbers = list(range(10))
for i in numbers:
    if numbers[i] == 5:
        numbers.remove(i)

# Exercise 2

TRY-EXCEPTAt least one of us entered our email in a wrong form to an app or a website once. In such a situation, you usally

Suppose you want to draw a million stars. It’s take forever to complete this task unless you, I guess, desire to be a professional star drawer. There must be a way to avoid such an endlessly repetitive action. Exactly, it’s a loop, which repeats some action within itself. In Python, there are two types of loops including for and while loops.

:mag_right: For Loop

# code before for

for element in iterable:
    # code inside for

# code after for
  • A for loop is used when the number of times you want to iterate over a sequence (a.k.a, an iterable).
  • An iterable can be a string, list, dictionary, tuple, and range().
  • An element’s name can be almost anything but is usually i or _.

For now, we’ll focus on the range(start, stop, step) function.

  • start is 0 and step is 1 by default. Passing arguments to these parameters is optional.
  • The stop value is required.
  • The loop runs through range() from start up to but not including stop.

Let’s look at some examples.

range(3) range(1, 8, 3)
  1. range(3) starts at 0, ends by 3, and increases by 1:
    • 0 < 3 true -> add 1 to 0, get 1
    • 1 < 3 true -> add 1 to 1, get 2
    • 2 < 3 true -> add 1 to 2, get 3
    • 3 < 3 false -> stop
    So range(3) contains 0, 1, and 2.
  2. range(1, 8, 3) starts at 1, ends by 8, and increases by 3:
    • 1 < 8 true -> add 3 to 1, get 4
    • 4 < 8 true -> add 3 to 4, get 7
    • 7 < 8 true -> add 3 to 7, get 10
    • 10 < 8 false -> stop
    So range(1, 8, 3) contains 1, 4, and 7.
# repeat 3 times
for i in range(3):
print(i)
range(3) contains 0, 1, and 2.
  • i = 0 < 3 true -> print(0) -> add 1 to i = 0, get i = 1
  • i = 1 < 3 true -> print(1) -> add 1 to i = 1, get i = 2
  • i = 2 < 3 true -> print(2) -> add 1 to i = 2, get i = 3
  • i = 3 < 3 false -> stop -> display the rendered output
The rendered output is
0
1
2
# repeat 3 times
value = 5
for i in range(3):
print(value + i)
range(3) contains 0, 1, and 2.
  • i = 0 < 3 true -> print(5 + 0) -> add 1 to i = 0, get i = 1
  • i = 1 < 3 true -> print(5 + 1) -> add 1 to i = 1, get i = 2
  • i = 2 < 3 true -> print(5 + 2) -> add 1 to i = 2, get i = 3
  • i = 3 < 3 false -> stop -> display the rendered output
The rendered output is
5
6
7
Accumulation Pattern for Summation # repeat 5 times
total = 0
for i in range(5):
total = total + i
print(total)
range(5) contains 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4.
  • i = 0 < 5 true -> total = 0 + 0 -> print(0) -> add 1 to i = 0, get i = 1
  • i = 1 < 5 true -> total = 0 + 1 -> print(1) -> add 1 to i = 1, get i = 2
  • i = 2 < 5 true -> total = 1 + 2 -> print(3) -> add 1 to i = 2, get i = 3
  • i = 3 < 5 true -> total = 3 + 3 -> print(6) -> add 1 to i = 3, get i = 4
  • i = 4 < 5 true -> total = 6 + 4 -> print(10) -> add 1 to i = 4, get i = 5
  • i = 5 < 5 false -> stop -> display the rendered output
The rendered output is
0
1
3
6
10
Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: How is this loop different from the summation example? for i in range(5): total = 0 total = total + i print(total)
Exercise 2: Do these for loop calculate the product of numbers from 1 to 5 (i.e., the factorial of 5)? Explain why or why not. How can you make a loop that use accumulation pattern to compute the product? product = 0 for i in range(5): product = product * i print(product) product = 1 for i in range(5): product = product * i print(product)
Exercise 3: What should you pay attention to when applying the accumulation pattern?

:mag_right: While Loops

# code before while

while condition:
    # code inside while

# code after while
  • A while loop is used when you don’t know the number of iterations.
  • A while loop runs as long as conditions are fulfilled. :warning: Always update conditions inside the loop. Or else, you may create/encounter an infinite loop which runs forever unless you force it to quit.

:mag_right: Keywords Used in Loops

:stop_sign: break

Imagine you are playing “Where’s Waldo?” and know exactly how many objects there are on the page. You want to look through images and stop the puzzle once you find Waldo. Or you could imagine you are playing a game where you have to guess a number. You’d have to keep guessing until you get the correct one; this is when the program would release you. Clearly, you need to use a loop to do iterations in each case, but you want a stronger command to leave when getting what you came for. Yup, it’s a break!

The break keyword is mainly used to terminate a loop regardless of whether a for loop iterates over the whole range or the condition in a while loop may still be satisfied. Simply put, when the program hits the break keyword, it breaks out of the loop.

Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: Do these for loops give the same result? Explain why or why not. for x in range(7): print(x) if x == 5: break print("iloveaivietnam") for x in range(7): if x == 5: break print(x) print("iloveaivietnam")
Exercise 2: Understand this while loop and modify itp to see how many times you need to roll a dice to get a six. import random while True: roll = random.randint(1, 6) print(f"You rolled {roll}.) if roll == 6: print("You win!") break
Exercise 3: Give an example where you can replace a for loop with break with a while loop?
Exercise 4: In which case do you think you have to use while loop with break instead of whle loop? Can you give an example?

:repeat: continue

Imagine you are building a machine that would pick up only ripe strawberries and skip unripe ones without stopping. Here, a loop can handle part of the requirements and needs a magic word to fulfil what you expect. Such a magic word is continue.

The continue keyword is to skip the rest of the steps in this turn and move on with the next round. It is less common than the break keyword.

Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: In which case is the continue keyword needed? for x in range(7): print(x) if x == 5: continue print("iloveaivietnam") for x in range(7): if x == 5: continue print(x) print("iloveaivietnam")
Exercise 2: Rewrite the code of exercise 1 with the while loop.

:mag_right: Examples and Exercises

Estimate the Area of a Unit Circle.
***Problem: Design a Loss Function*** p is probability of something happen need to design function f(p) describes the level of your surprise. the more surprised you are, the larger f(p) is. experiment 2 is more surprising probability of something happen or our believe is disproportional to the level of your surprises i.e reciprocal the lower probability, the more surprised can be 1-p (linear) or 1/p(nonlinear) but nonlinear has more interesting properties/characteristics. so we choose s=surprise=1/p p in [0,1] so s=1/p in [1, inf] done however, we still want to improve this because s=1/p in [1,inf] means s=1/p=1 means no surprise, which is mathematically strange. we want s=0. we can minus, but come on, we have something better and we learned just now. yup it's logarithm. so we choose f(p)=log(1/p) in [0, inf] thanks to its monotone, f(p) is proportional to s=surprise=1/p which means both can interpret the level of surprise let's look deeper. in terms of graph, when taking log, the result is significantly lower (smaller) than s=1/p or 1/p-1, which is more convinient to compute. this function is called information used in information theory
Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: PI Estimation (Gregory-Leibniz Series) $$\text{PI} \approx 4 \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{(-1)^{i+1}}{2i-1}$$
Exercise 2: PI Estimation (Nilakantha Series) $$\text{PI} \approx 3 + 4 \sum_{i=0}^{n} \frac{(-1)^{i}}{(2i+2)(2i+3)(2i+4)}$$
Exercise 3: Quadratic Root (Newton Method)
The Newton Method can be used to approximate a root of $f(x) = 0$ by the general formula $$x_{n+1} = x_{n} - \frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_{n})}.$$ Generate a mathematical formula for $f(x) = x^2 - a$ to approximate $\sqrt{a}$. Rewrite the formula in a programming fashion. Write a function that $a$ and $n$ and returns $\sqrt{a}$.
Exercise 4: Write a function the compute the factorial of a positive number using a loop.
Exercise 5: Write a function the compute the factorial of a non-negative number using a loop.
Exercise 6: Give possible mistakes one might make when writing a factorial function.

:speech_balloon: FAQ

Here are some good questions asked during class. The answers to these questions came from either some admin, TA, STA, or members of AIO2025.

Questions Answers
Can I call a function before defining it? No. Python reads code top-down.
Can I write 2 functions A and B where A calls B and B calls A? Why does it give an error when I refer to one before defining it? Yes. Such a situation is called mutual recursion. Python doesn’t execute function definitions which consist of function references. It only starts evaluating when a function is called.

entry.title: Python for AI 101
entry.content:
:round_pushpin: Acknowledgement: This post is based mainly on Dr. Quang-Vinh Dinh’s presentation and slides and partly on peers’ responses from the course, AIO2025, offered by AI VIETNAM.

:thought_balloon: Relevant information and opinions: The audience of this lecture were those who know nothing about coding, have some coding experience, and know a bit of AI knowledge. It is reccommended that complete newbies should read the materials and spend time practicing writing code without the assistance of AI over and over again to improve their coding and code-reading skills. Note that only necessary Python knowledge is introduced here.

Making an error while coding is, in fact, a good sign which reccommends you keep going to figure out what the problem is and how to resolve it. -Dr. Quang-Vinh Dinh

In today’s post, we’ll look at some basic Python for AI including data representation, functions, and conditions.

Before getting into the main materials, I cannot stress enough how important it is to comment on your code.

:pushpin: Pro tip: Annotate your code - always!
Keeping documentation of what your code does is far more important than most people might think. Your log isn’t for today but tomorrow. It benefits not only future you but your colleagues or anyone else trying to read or maintain your code.

  • Use # for single-line comments
  • Use ''' or """ for multi-line comments and docstrings.

:mag_right: Introduction

We consider Python as a tool that alllows us to transform our ideas into a program producing desired results. Don’t worry about becoming an expert in Python since it, just like other programming languages, is a means of solving problems but a goal to reach. Essentially, you need to know its syntax and structure.

It’s usually easier to learn something when we know its history and why it is studied or used. The same goes for Python. Python is extensively adopted in the community of data science and machine learning because it has a giant and vibrant ecosystem with plentiful frameworks, libraries, and packages which are of diferrent purposes. Some examples can be found in the table below.

Purposes Frameworks Libraries Packages
Scientific Computing   Pandas NumPy
Visualization   matplotlib, plotly  
Machine Learning and Deep Learning TensorFlow, Pytorch Keras  
Natural Language Processing   Natural Language Toolkit (NLTK), GENSIM, spaCy  


To write and run a program in Python, you can choose among some options such as Google Colab, Jupyter, Visual Studio Code, and PyCharm. It’s not difficult to look for a video or post which guides you install and/or use them.

python history

:mag_right: Data Representation

In Python, data can be represented in various ways which are sorted into three groups discussed below. To work with data in any programming language, it is imperative that it be stored to a variable. That way, you can refer to and work with such a variable later on. In Python, the syntax to define a variable is simple.

variable_name = variable_value

You may want to think of a variable as a container, a variable name as the container’s name, and a variable value as what is inside that container. You are allowed to use and/or modify the value as needed. For instance,

mystery_box = "IPhone"

# a container called *mystery_box* has a value of *"IPhone"* in it.

Now, you may ask: What can I can name a variable? Are there any conventions I should be aware of? A few thing is worth mentioning regarding the varibale name.

  • Meaningful name: Even though you can name a variable whatever you want, it makes sense to give a name relevant to its purpose.
  • snake_case:
  • Avoid keyword: A syntax error is returned as a keyword is used as a variable. Usually, the editor you use displays a red squiggly underline under such a variable name.

:one: Primitive Data Types

There are three main categories of primitive data types including logic, number, and text.


Note that quotations used in a string must be uniform, that is, a text starts with a double quotation must end with one rather than a single quotation.

:heavy_exclamation_mark: Overflow and Underflow

No matter how much a language’s memory is extended, their size is always limited or blocked on both sides. This means a computer’s memory cannot represent too large or too small numbers. These situations are called overflow and underflow, respectively. Python returns inf for the former and 0.0 for the latter.

:bulb: Application in AI

As you may know, a computer can only understand numbers, therefore, it is a must to convert texts into numbers so that the computer system and network can tackle. This is a common NLP task; an example that you may know is Google Translate.

:two: More Abstract Data Structure

Just as their name suggest, primitive data representation can only support basic jobs. To handle more complex assignment, we need (built-in) multiplex structures such as list and fonary. Here, we’ll just get to know their definitions and discuss them in detail in .

:heavy_check_mark: List

list_name = [element_1, ..., element_n]

In addition to their values, each element is associated to an index which is automatically created when the list is defined. Forward indices start at 0 for the first element on the left and increase one by one till the end of the list. In practice, you get to elements’ values via their indices. Let’s take a look at an example.

    # create a list of fruits
    fruits = ["apple", "orange", "banana", "grape", "mango"]

    fruits[0]
    >>> "apple"
    fruits[2]
    >>> "banana"

    '''
    +-------+-------+--------+--------+-------+-------+
    | Fruit | apple | orange | banana | grape | mango |
    +=======+=======+========+========+=======+=======+
    | Index |   0   |   1    |   2    |   3   |   4   |
    +-------+-------+--------+--------+-------+-------+

    +---------+-------+
    | Fruit   | Index |
    +=========+=======+
    | "apple" |   0   |
    +---------+-------+
    | "orange"|   1   |
    +---------+-------+
    | "banana"|   2   |
    +---------+-------+
    | "grapes"|   3   |
    +---------+-------+
    | "mango" |   4   |
    +---------+-------+

    - 0 → apple 🍎
    - 1 → orange 🍊
    - 2 → banana 🍌
    - 3 → grape 🍇
    - 4 → mango 🥭
    '''

DEMONSTRATION

Of course, elements of a list can be logic, numbers, and more.

    data = [5, 4.7, -2, "hello", 0, True, -1000.1]

:heavy_check_mark: Dictionary

dictionary_name = {key_1: value_1, ..., key_n: value_n}

Another prevalent data structure is dictionary. When you look up a word in a regular-sense dictionary, you’ll see two parts: the word and its meaning(s); no word appears more than once in a dictionary. A dictionary in Python is created in a similar fashion with unique keys and a value for each of them. Take the following example.

# create a dictionary of a fruit's characteristics
fruit = {"name": "avocado", "type": "berry", "nutrition": ["fat", "fiber", "vitamins"], 7: 100}

fruit[7]
>>> 100
fruit["nutrition"]
>>> ["fat", "fiber", "vitamins"]

As seen above, in a dictionary, an element’s value can be retrieved using its key in lieu of index.

:three: Other Data Representation

:bar_chart: Tabular and :framed_picture: Image Data are predominant in data analysis. They are both handled using matrix formats.

:mag_right: Functions

def function_name(parameter_1, ..., parameter_n):
    '''
    do docstring here.
    '''

    code here

    return result

:heavy_check_mark: Why do we need functions?

DEMONSTRATION WITH A MAGIC BOX Let’s say you want a machine to make a sandwich every morning.

:one: It’d be time-consuming to place every single step in the machine every day just to make the same sandwich. You want it to receive one line of request and automatically undertake all the tasks. What can make this happen? Exactly, a function. It allows us to reuse the same block of codes as wanted without writing them all out.

:two: Possible steps to complete this job can be grouped into two main parts as in the table below. It’s much clearer separating the tasks because we know exactly how to allocate one block of time to a set of actions. Of course, you can certainly put all the actions in one function, but you need to work on both its and the program’s logic when changing any code inside.

Get the ingredients Put the ingredients together
Get two slice of breads Use the knife to spread peanut butter on one side of a slice
Get the peanut butter container Use the knife to spread peanut butter on one side of the other slice
Get a knife Put the peanut butter sides of two slices together


:heavy_check_mark: What is a function?

DEMONSTRATION WITH BLENDER, INPUT, EXAMPLE

  • A function takes inputs, do something within itself, and returns outputs. There are situations where no inputs or outputs are fed to a function.
  • A function must start with the def keyword and is reccomended to end with the return keyword when defined. If none is expected to be returned, put return None.
  • A function’s body must be indented.
  • A function is frequently named with a verb to indicate its action and written in snake_case.
  • A function’s parameters can be set to default values but passing different arguments to such parameters are allowed. Default values are often placed at the end of a parameter set.

examples maybe

:heavy_check_mark: Types of Functions

There are two main types of functions including built-in functions and user-defined functions.

:one: Built-in Funtions

Built-in functions are created by and freely available to the Python community. Two common built-in functions are print and type. The former displays output and the latter returns the type of a given variable.

Besides functions used without further concerns, there are functions that can only be executed with packages called module like random and math. Use the import keyword to access modules. Try and see what the code below gives you.

import math

x = 4
y = -3

print(math.sqrt(x))
print(math.sqrt(y))
print(math.fabs(x))
print(math.fabs(y))
print(math.log(math.e))  # log is based e
:bulb: Application in AI

:heavy_check_mark: Square Root Function
A square root function is used in object detection problems how much an object moves is relative its size and the function is to deal with this challenge.

:heavy_check_mark: Logarithm Function
:abacus: Logarithm has $\log({1}) = 0$ and is a monotonically increasing function, i.e., $f(x_1) < f(x_2) \text{ when } x_1 < x_2$.

These properties extensively used in optimization algorithms problems which are ubiquitous in machine learning. For example, in a situation where we maximize a function, evaluating log of the function is computationally easier than the function itself while taking its log does not change the maximum’s position.

DEMONSTRATION WITH PICTURE OF F(X) AND LOG(F(X))

Now you may ask:

:one: When do I use the log function?
The short answer is when you only care about the value of a number compared to that of another rather than their actual values. Since log of a number approaches $\infty$ and $-\infty$ much more slowly than the number goes to $\infty$ and $0$, respectively, the program can easily avoid the overflow and underflow issues.

CODE DEMONSTRATION

:two: How do I know which function(s) to use provided a problem?
That’s a great question! Let’s look at an example and we’ll walk through the thought process to develop and improve a solution.

Design a Loss Function
***Problem: Design a Loss Function*** p is probability of something happen need to design function f(p) describes the level of your surprise. the more surprised you are, the larger f(p) is. experiment 2 is more surprising probability of something happen or our believe is disproportional to the level of your surprises i.e reciprocal the lower probability, the more surprised can be 1-p (linear) or 1/p(nonlinear) but nonlinear has more interesting properties/characteristics. so we choose s=surprise=1/p p in [0,1] so s=1/p in [1, inf] done however, we still want to improve this because s=1/p in [1,inf] means s=1/p=1 means no surprise, which is mathematically strange. we want s=0. we can minus, but come on, we have something better and we learned just now. yup it's logarithm. so we choose f(p)=log(1/p) in [0, inf] thanks to its monotone, f(p) is proportional to s=surprise=1/p which means both can interpret the level of surprise let's look deeper. in terms of graph, when taking log, the result is significantly lower (smaller) than s=1/p or 1/p-1, which is more convinient to compute. this function is called information used in information theory


:heavy_check_mark: Exponential Function
:abacus: An exponential function $\exp({x})$ has a range of $(0, \infty)$ when $x$ is in $(-\infty, \infty)$.

This property allows an exponential function to be used in the Softmax function. This function determines how related an object and its background in an image are. For example, (positive relation) a rabbit and a bush ir a snake and a bush have a postive relation; fish and a bush have a negative relation (you may convince me otherwise if you show me evidence where alive fish is on land).

Design the Softmax Function
compute percentage assumption for a regular case is that x_i >= 0 for percentage computation makes sense but our problem is that x_i in (-inf,inf). to deal with our problem, we need to make negative x_i's >= 0 to do so, we use exponential function since exp(x) in (0,inf) where x in (-inf,inf) so we get softmax function used in machine learning. we can use different base but e is standard

code -> overflow error - explained in further reading

:two: User-defined Functions

CODE compute salary - don’t forget to comment

function computer_salary is canceled once it finishes one computation/returns function is like a room in the main house return -> needs to have a basket to receive and carry that result can reuse variable

CODE estimate area of circle error -> reduce error -> alpha goes to 0

:mag_right: Branching/Conditions

Conditional statements in Python enables the execution of certain code blocks based on whether a condition is true or false.

:heavy_check_mark: Comparison Operators

Comparison operators are symbols used to compare two values and create a condition for a conditional statement.

Operator Math Meaning
$==$ $=$ Equal
$!=$ $\neq$ Not equal
$>$ $>$ Greater than
$<$ $<$ Less than
$>=$ $\geq$ Greater than or equal
$<=$ $\leq$ Less than or equal


:heavy_check_mark: Basic Conditional Statements

Imagine there are two or three doors and you have a key that can unlock exactly one of them. You need to check one by one and once you open the right door, you can walk through without checking the rest.

To understand the process of these conditional statements, let’s look at their flowcharts which use shapes and arrows to depict steps and decisions.

DEMONSTRATION STATEMENTS SIDE BY SIDE ONLY

:one: If

:two: If-Else

:three: If-Elif-Else

EXAMPLE FOR IF ELIF ELSE

Practice Exercises
relu(x), rule based chatbot, discussion

hàm log ánh xạ tính chat với hàm gốc

khi tập dataset bao gồm cả số âm và dương nên dung hàm mũ

khi hàm mũ quá lớn sẽ bị overflow -> sử dung SoftMax function tránh tình trạng này

Q: tsao mô hình làm việc với số mà ko làm việc với text ạ? A: bạn hiểu nôm na là máy tính chỉ hiểu và xây dựng dựa trên 2 con số 1 vs 0, ghép các số này lại mình được số nhị phân -> số thập phân -> mã hóa thành text ta hiểu - Pham Hoa Nhan

:speech_balloon: FAQ

Here are some good questions asked during class. The answers to these questions came from either some admin, TA, STA, or members of AIO2025.

Questions Answers
Does a program run the comments? No. The comments are only for the owners and readers.
What are real-life applications of a logarithm function? Information theory (entropy), Astronomy (lights’ and stars’ brightness), Machine learning (logistic regression, cross-entropy)
What are values modified for? Value modification is to avoid disadvantageous scenarios like overflow, underflow, slow computations, errors, divergent sequences. Some functions are used to change the range so that values are easier to be dealt with but still preserve core characteristics.
If one module needs a supporting one, do I need to import the latter? No. Modules consist of their supporting modules.
Where do I look for a function that I need? dir() shows attributes of an object or help() provides detailed documentation.

I finally finished my very first post for the course I’m taking, AIO2025, after 5 days of semi-hard work. Well, for more context, I set it up and wrote about one quarter of the whole post and stop for a couple of days before picking it up again today. It took me 4 days to clone this repository and set up the website (partially) with the help of my friend, J. (I don’t know if my friend wants to have the name public, so let me not do it). I’m behind on the lecture summarization and I’m far from having my website ready to the public. But, it’s okay; I’m just glad that I get one important thing done and want to briefly reward myself with avocado banana smoothie. I deliberately used half a banana as an alternative to sugar, condensed milk, or sweetened milk, but my smoothie turned out to be extremely sweet. I guess it’s for my tiny achievement. :smiley:

I’ve learned a lot about using Markdown while making this first post. The whole writing process reminded me of the time I learned LaTex. You know, just jumping right in the battle field and googling ways to win it. It can be complicated, but I have not needed anything terribly challenging up to this point. Of course,there are stylings or decorations I hope to make so my blog does not look so dull. But what I have so far is acceptable for a complete newbie like me. I’ll learn more along the way and the journey will be much fun.

Let’s go back to what I learned:

:heavy_check_mark: A list for Markdown

  • Create internal and external links
  • Create a list
  • Create a table and incorporate CSS to style it
  • Use emojis

Initially, I didn’t think about using emojis at all, but I consulted this really cool post. There are a bunch of features here I want to incorporate into my posts. It will be a task for the future though.

:heavy_check_mark: A list for English

  • integrate and incorporate
  • efficient and effective

As a non-native English speaker, I always find it challenging using English in the most natural way. It takes a bit of time to look up words with similar meaning and then figure out which word is suitable for some situatuion. To avoid being stressed out while doing so, I try to think of it as an opportunity for me to improve not only writing skills but also translating ones. Soon I’ll get better at these skills. :muscle:

Anyway, I think it’s time to be away from the screen for a bit and then start the second post.

entry.title: Research Anything AI 101
entry.content:
:round_pushpin: Acknowledgement: This post is based entirely on Dr. Vinh Dinh’s presentation and slides from the course, AIO2025, offered by AI VIETNAM.

:thought_balloon: Relevant information and opinions: The audience of this lecture were those who start setting foot into the world of AI and pursue industrial or academic research in this field. However, skills mentioned here, I think, should be applicable to anyone who desires to learn and explore a subject in depth.

In today’s post, we’ll look at some necessary skills that a person is encouraged to learn as the first chapter of doing research in the AI field or even any field.

:mag_right: How to Find Scientific Documents/Papers

Having the right materials to read up besides textbooks or lecture notes is crucial while you study or research any subject. However, such materials do not just magically appear in front of us. You need to not only dig through the internet for them but make sure their origins are reliable as well. There are two primary types of resources that scholars use to suppport their projects including published literature and preprints. We will now talk about where to obtain them and what their differences are in terms of reliability.

:one: Published Literature

Published literature refers to peer-reviewed sources which are formally released by recognized publishing companies and made available to the public. Here are several places where such documents/papers in the field of AI can be found using keywords.

:heavy_check_mark: Google Scholar:

Google Scholar is the first go-to webiste for researchers of all areas. This is a fast and straightforward way to learn about articles suitable for your research works. The website provides the sources of most (if not all) academic papers with different versions or publishers and related information. You can narrow down results by using year filters. Say, when you are looking for a literature review/survey since it’s recommneded at papers printed within the last 3-5 years.

:heavy_check_mark: IEEE:

IEEE contains scientific and technical documents issued by itself and its partners. Using this website, you can look for related publications based on its content type such as conferences and journals, its affiliation,and many more.

:heavy_check_mark: PubMed

PubMed is a free database for those interested in using AI in biomedical and life sciences. Readers can While full-text archives by PubMed Central (PMC) are free, access to other publishers’s articles may require a fee.

:heavy_check_mark: Other Resources

Springer, ScienceDirect, and Elsevier are some trusted publishers that you can reach when it comes to scientific papers of any field.

:two: Preprints

Even though published literature are validated resources, the peer review and editting process can take about 3-6 months or even a year or more. It means researchers do not have full accesss to up-to-date techniques, which delays the whole research community’s progress. With that in mind, scholars created sites allowing people to post their research works before or while they are submitted to a journal or conference. Keep in mind that these papers may introduce the lastest methods, but they might not have been evaluated by experts yet. Here are a few popular places where preprints can be checked out.

:heavy_check_mark: https://arxiv.org/

More than 2 million scholarly articles in the field of physics, mathematics, computer science, quantitative biology, quantitative finance, statistics, electrical engineering and systems science, and economics are freely accessible through this website.

:heavy_check_mark: https://www.biorxiv.org/

A wide range of preprints and archives in biology and life sciences are commonly found in this website. A link to the formal version of these materials can be found here within weeks of its publication.

:heavy_check_mark: Papers with Code

Papers with Code is a free and open resource specifically for Machine Learning papers. Even though the site does not require the corresponding code implementations upon submission, source code and datasets are suggested being included. This is a great way for readers to understand, reproduce, and improve ideas and experiments presented in these research articles.

:mag_right: How to Read Scientific Documents/Papers

While both scientific papers and essays heavily involve writing, it’s worth noting that they are quite disparate. In few words, scientific papers are factual whereas essays’ tone is biased. The table below comprises key differences between the two.

  Scientific Papers Essays
Purpose contribute new knowledge to a specific field argue a point, explore a topic, or reflect on an issue
Target audience scholars, researchers, scientists, and professionals general audience or special readers
Focus empirical evidence, methodologies, and data analysis critical thinking, analysis, and personal perspectives
Structure introduction, literature review, methodology, findings, and conclusion introduction, body, and conclusion


:pushpin: Reading a research paper can be a challenge, especially to those who do it for the very first time; it can even take them a month to understand one. It is not uncommon since there are so many new terms and algorithms an absolute beginner needs to learn from references. If you are a newbie in a field, you should not be discouraged because it will get better; the amount of time you need to spend reading later papers will be significantly better.

If you are totally new to research (like me), you may have a few questions in mind like: Do I read from beginning to end? Do I try to understand every single detail? Do I only read some parts? If so, what do I choose and what do I ignore? All these boil down to one common concern: How do I read a research paper efficiently? We’ll now discuss Dr. Vinh Dinh’s reading technique based on his first-hand experience step by step.

:zero: Title

The very first thing you should do when picking up a paper is to read its title. The title consists of keywords that helps determine whether a paper matches your research topic or not. If the title has or is related to the name of ideas or techniques you are interested in, you can move to the next step. Otherwise, you can pass.

:one: Abstract

Once you’re good to move forward, go ahead and read its abstract. The abstract is considered the essense of an article, summarizing every remaining section within 250-300 words. It enables you quickly assess its relevance and value to your work so you can decide if the paper is worth your effort.

:two: Introduction

If the abstract is intriguing, start reading the introduction section. The introduction shows you the big piture of what this research is about. Here you’ll learn about the research background context, and question which all help layout the paper’s structure and main arguments. Basically, this is where scholars sell their papers.

:three: Experimental Result

It is imperative that you read this section right after the introduction because how they advertise their “product” and how good their ideas are may not be what you are looking for. You’d like to know if what the authors propose is actually practicable in your case and provides the result meets your expectations. This section may contain data visualizations and statistics helping you make a decision. The idea is for you to skip some long parts of the paper that may be unnecessary to you.

:four: The Proposed Method

If you’re satisfied with the result, you can go back to the proposed method to learn how they produce, brainstorm, and implement their innovative ideas to resolve their research problem. Note that it may take up to a couple of weeks to grasp the picture. Also, you won’t, most of the times, be able to comprehend their method immediately. That’s when you read the related works or look up references.

:five: Related Works

This section is a survey of previously related works and their drawbacks. Readers can refer to this part and the Reference section to obtain relevant knowledge, techniques, and algorithms.

:heavy_check_mark: NotebookLM and Prompting Skills

We’re talking about doing research in AI; why not make good use of the product of the field? NotebookLM allows you to upload a scientific paper and assists you with summarizing the paper or explaining a concept. Incorporating this site into your study can speed up the process quite a bit.

To utilize this tool effeciently, you need to have or learn prompoting skills. Without a SMART question, an AI assistant may yield results that are too broad/general or have incorrect attached resources. These skills will be discussed later in the course.

How to Make a Research Plan

Similar to reading a scientific paper, you can use AI to learn AI when it comes to making a research plan. One recommended AI assisting you to complete this task is Gemini Deep Research. It can generate a detailed document with just a simple prompt: “I want to conduct research on object detection using deep learning models; help me write a research plan.” You can try and see what it can do.

Where to Implement Your Code

You have ideas; you want to put it into action. Here are a couple of places where you can do so.

:heavy_check_mark: Jupyter Notebook

You can use it via either Python Compiler or Anaconda. The latter one has various tools in addition to Jupyter Notebook and is easier to install. Since this is run locally and AI training requires GPUs with high VRAM, you computer’s system resourcess might not be sufficient. Google Colab, which is mentioned below, can resolve this issue to a large extent.

:heavy_check_mark: Google Colab

Google Colab provides free limited (but enough to start with) online resources. You just need to connect with your gmail account and begin using it without any installation. This site allows you to mount your notebooks to Google Drive or Github and download/upload them to/from your computer as well as has Gemini AI available. In Colab, your code runs on CPU by default; however, you can change runtime type to GPU or TPU.

:robot: Speaking of Gemini AI coding assistant, it’s worth mentioning two other popular ones, ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot, and what they can do for you. Of course, this again requires your prompting skills.

  • :gear: Generate a sample code: “Generate a Python example that uses Matplotlib and plotsa square function from -10 to 10.”
  • :ladder: Explain an existing code step by step.
  • :memo: Add comments to an existing code.
  • :beetle: Debug an existing code and suggest a solution: “This program has anunexpected result. Find it out.”
  • :hammer_and_wrench: Design a solution for a program based on a prompt or paper: “I havean ID array of numbers. I want to get themaximum number. Design an algorithm and give apseudo-code using Pythonic style.”
  • :question: Explain concepts: “What is theLambda function in Python?”

I encourage all of us try prompts out with AI and see how it performs and how you can make it work better for us.

:warning: While AI assistants can help you learn coding faster, overreliance on AI can reduce your criticalthinking and programming skills if you firstlearn coding.

You should verify anything AI assistants provide. They are just your assistants! They can be wrong. -Dr. Dinh Vinh

How to Document Your Results

While you can use Microsoft Word to make a document, it’s probably universal that scholars document their research works using LaTeX, which is more convenient for professionals to create scientific and technical content.

:heavy_check_mark: You can download softwares like MikTex and TeXworks (included in MikTex’s package) to use and preview offline.

:heavy_check_mark: You can also write LaTex online using Overleaf. The perk of using this is that it allows multiple collaborators to edit on the same file simultaneously.

:speech_balloon: FAQ

Here are some good questions asked during class. The answers to these questions came from either some admin, TA, STA, or members of AIO2025.

Questions Answers
A project may have a large file of codes and repositories. Where do I start to read? How can I find its codebase? Repomix packs the source code into one .xml file which you can ask AI to identify the codebase.
How can I use Markdown? Markdown Cheat Sheet
what do I start with when using Overleaf? AIO Template by TA Nha and LaTex Cheat Sheet
Where do I start when it comes to coding, specifically Python? Python Tutorials w3schools, Python Tutorials YouTube, and Python 35 Days
I want to review math for machine learning. Which resources can I use? Mathematics for Machine Learning

entry.title: Google Gemini updates: Flash 1.5, Gemma 2 and Project Astra

link.title: Google Gemini updates: Flash 1.5, Gemma 2 and Project Astra

entry.content:
May 14, 2024[[read-time]] min read We’re introducing a series of updates across the Gemini family of models, including the new 1.5 Flash, our lightweight model for speed and efficiency, and Project Astra, our vision for the future of AI assistants. In December, we launched our first natively multimodal model Gemini 1.0 in three sizes: Ultra, Pro and Nano. Just a few months later we released 1.5 Pro, with enhanced performance and a breakthrough long context window of 1 million tokens.Developers and enterprise customers have been putting 1.5 Pro to use in incredible ways and finding its long context window, multimodal reasoning capabilities and impressive overall performance incredibly useful.We know from user feedback that some applications need lower latency and a lower cost to serve. This inspired us to keep innovating, so today, we’re introducing Gemini 1.5 Flash: a model that’s lighter-weight than 1.5 Pro, and designed to be fast and efficient to serve at scale.Both 1.5 Pro and 1.5 Flash are available in public preview with a 1 million token context window in Google AI Studio and Vertex AI. And now, 1.5 Pro is also available with a 2 million token context window via waitlist to developers using the API and to Google Cloud customers.We’re also introducing updates across the Gemini family of models, announcing our next generation of open models, Gemma 2, and sharing progress on the future of AI assistants, with Project Astra.Context lengths of leading foundation models compared with Gemini 1.5’s 2 million token capability1.5 Flash is the newest addition to the Gemini model family and the fastest Gemini model served in the API. It’s optimized for high-volume, high-frequency tasks at scale, is more cost-efficient to serve and features our breakthrough long context window.While it’s a lighter weight model than 1.5 Pro, it’s highly capable of multimodal reasoning across vast amounts of information and delivers impressive quality for its size.The new Gemini 1.5 Flash model is optimized for speed and efficiency, is highly capable of multimodal reasoning and features our breakthrough long context window.1.5 Flash excels at summarization, chat applications, image and video captioning, data extraction from long documents and tables, and more. This is because it’s been trained by 1.5 Pro through a process called “distillation,” where the most essential knowledge and skills from a larger model are transferred to a smaller, more efficient model.Read more about 1.5 Flash in our updated Gemini 1.5 technical report, on the Gemini technology page, and learn about 1.5 Flash’s availability and pricing.Over the last few months, we’ve significantly improved 1.5 Pro, our best model for general performance across a wide range of tasks.Beyond extending its context window to 2 million tokens, we’ve enhanced its code generation, logical reasoning and planning, multi-turn conversation, and audio and image understanding through data and algorithmic advances. We see strong improvements on public and internal benchmarks for each of these tasks.1.5 Pro can now follow increasingly complex and nuanced instructions, including ones that specify product-level behavior involving role, format and style. We’ve improved control over the model’s responses for specific use cases, like crafting the persona and response style of a chat agent or automating workflows through multiple function calls. And we’ve enabled users to steer model behavior by setting system instructions.We added audio understanding in the Gemini API and Google AI Studio, so 1.5 Pro can now reason across image and audio for videos uploaded in Google AI Studio. And we’re now integrating 1.5 Pro into Google products, including Gemini Advanced and in Workspace apps.Read more about 1.5 Pro in our updated Gemini 1.5 technical report and on the Gemini technology page.Gemini Nano is expanding beyond text-only inputs to include images as well. Starting with Pixel, applications using Gemini Nano with Multimodality will be able to understand the world the way people do — not just through text, but also through sight, sound and spoken language.Read more about Gemini 1.0 Nano on Android.Today, we’re also sharing a series of updates to Gemma, our family of open models built from the same research and technology used to create the Gemini models.We’re announcing Gemma 2, our next generation of open models for responsible AI innovation. Gemma 2 has a new architecture designed for breakthrough performance and efficiency, and will be available in new sizes.The Gemma family is also expanding with PaliGemma, our first vision-language model inspired by PaLI-3. And we’ve upgraded our Responsible Generative AI Toolkit with LLM Comparator for evaluating the quality of model responses.Read more on the Developer blog.As part of Google DeepMind’s mission to build AI responsibly to benefit humanity, we’ve always wanted to develop universal AI agents that can be helpful in everyday life. That’s why today, we’re sharing our progress in building the future of AI assistants with Project Astra (advanced seeing and talking responsive agent).To be truly useful, an agent needs to understand and respond to the complex and dynamic world just like people do — and take in and remember what it sees and hears to understand context and take action. It also needs to be proactive, teachable and personal, so users can talk to it naturally and without lag or delay.While we’ve made incredible progress developing AI systems that can understand multimodal information, getting response time down to something conversational is a difficult engineering challenge. Over the past few years, we’ve been working to improve how our models perceive, reason and converse to make the pace and quality of interaction feel more natural.Building on Gemini, we’ve developed prototype agents that can process information faster by continuously encoding video frames, combining the video and speech input into a timeline of events, and caching this information for efficient recall.By leveraging our leading speech models, we also enhanced how they sound, giving the agents a wider range of intonations. These agents can better understand the context they’re being used in, and respond quickly, in conversation.With technology like this, it’s easy to envision a future where people could have an expert AI assistant by their side, through a phone or glasses. And some of these capabilities are coming to Google products, like the Gemini app and web experience, later this year.We’ve made incredible progress so far with our family of Gemini models, and we’re always striving to advance the state-of-the-art even further. By investing in a relentless production line of innovation, we’re able to explore new ideas at the frontier, while also unlocking the possibility of new and exciting Gemini use cases.Learn more about Gemini and its capabilities. Your information will be used in accordance with Google’s privacy policy.

entry.title: a post with tabs
entry.content:
This is how a post with tabs looks like. Note that the tabs could be used for different purposes, not only for code.

First tabs

To add tabs, use the following syntax:

{% tabs group-name %}

{% tab group-name tab-name-1 %}

Content 1

{% endtab %}

{% tab group-name tab-name-2 %}

Content 2

{% endtab %}

{% endtabs %}

With this you can generate visualizations like:

  • php
  • js
  • ruby 
  • var_dump('hello');

  • console.log("hello");

  • pputs 'hello'

Another example

  • yaml
  • json 
  • hello:
  - "whatsup"
  - "hi"

  • {
  "hello": ["whatsup", "hi"]
}

Tabs for something else

  • text
  • quote
  • list

  • Regular text

  • A quote

  • Hipster list

    • brunch
    • fixie
    • raybans
    • messenger bag
